children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

They are in our homes, on our doorsteps and along our streets. From doorbells to traffic cameras, internet-connected cameras are becoming tools of modern warfare. Intelligence agencies and hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities to track enemy movements and identify targets. AI has made it easier to hack these cameras and analyze footage at scale.

Our reporters investigated the use of hacked cameras in conflicts from Ukraine to the Middle East, such as when hackers took control of a camera in Crimea and discovered a previously unknown Russian air base that Ukrainian forces later attacked.

With an estimated 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras worldwide, the vulnerabilities extend well beyond the battlefield. Weak passwords, outdated software and poor Wi-Fi security can leave your home cameras exposed. Read this to learn about protecting them from prying eyes.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES
Saudi Arabia closed Riyadh's international airport after a Houthi missile attack killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds.
America's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, boasted at Davos about her close ties to two Greek tycoons and said they were bankrolling her trips around the world.
President Trump called on Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelensky as its leader and piled pressure on Kyiv to stop airstrikes against Russian oil refineries.
The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine is facing a humanitarian crisis as mines and drones have cut off food deliveries and trapped residents.
EV-charging companies in the U.S. are on track to install about as many public electric-vehicle plugs this year as in 2025, despite a downturn in EV sales.
3. FROM THE MARKETS
Private-asset giants are using indexed annuities to tap retirement savings. The products have surged in popularity, helping fuel private lending to riskier companies.
As homeowners become more willing to cut prices, builders are seeing pressure on their already squeezed profit margins, writes Carol Ryan.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
The wave of unknown donors powering the rise of the new left.

In past elections, big donors to progressives were generally older, wealthy hippies or successful Hollywood players. Now, our analysis of campaign filings shows a crew of virtually unknown donors stepping in to fund the far left. The emerging group skews younger, is often South Asian or Middle Eastern, and works in fields such as technology and medicine. Many had never given to politics before last year, but they are now donating as much as $1 million each to fund progressive candidates and a new "anti-Aipac" super PAC, report Maggie Severns, Anthony DeBarros and Kara Dapena.
Silicon Valley's dream city crashes into small-town politics.

Ninety minutes from San Francisco, tech-backed entrepreneur Jan Sramek wants to build a walkable suburban utopia called California Forever. In 2024, developers pulled a ballot measure to exempt the project from county anti-sprawl rules when polling showed it heading for defeat. Now, internal emails show a bitter standoff between tech-backed developers and local county leaders that helped doom a $3 billion shipyard meant for the site, reports Zusha Elinson.

6. SEE THE STORY
Can wearables really track blood pressure without the cuff?

Nearly half of U.S. adults have high blood pressure, spurring a wave of health trackers from Apple, Google, Oura, Whoop and Hilo that promise insights without the anxiety-inducing arm squeeze. Our Personal Tech columnist Nicole Nguyen wore five of these devices for a month to test their claims. Check out what she learned, and why doctors warn these popular devices could give users a false sense of security.
7. HAPPENING THIS WEEK
Monday: The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences is announced. The IMF and World Bank kick off their annual meetings in Bangkok. Trump holds a rally in Ohio ahead of the midterms.
Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs report earnings, kicking off a busy week for big banks. Apple is expected to unveil new smart-home products. Trump holds a rally in Alaska.
Wednesday: The September consumer-price index is released. Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico participates in a CNN town hall. Trump holds a rally in Arizona.
Thursday: September producer-price and retail-sales data are released, offering a fresh look at inflation and consumer spending.
Friday: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak at the IMF's annual meetings. "You Can See Everything," a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, opens in theaters.
8. THE NUMBER

That is where forecasters expect the 10-year Treasury yield to end this year, up from a 4.4% projection in July, according to our latest survey of economists. Forecasters expect these higher yields to persist as a mix of improving growth, new inflationary pressures and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory forced them to re-evaluate assumptions about investor demand.
9. AND FINALLY...
The "Sunday scaries" are real, and they are getting worse.

That sinking feeling of dread as the weekend winds down has become so pervasive that Merriam-Webster recently added the term to its online dictionary. As workloads mount and job security ebbs, employees are logging in on Sundays to tackle unfinished tasks. Some are fighting back with strict limits on weekend work, including one woman who bought a $30 hourglass to limit her Sunday work to 60 minutes.
